brief: Given r red, g green and b blue balloons, form as many tables as possible, each with exactly three balloons that are not all one colour.
key_idea: Answer = min(total/3, total - largest colour): every table needs a balloon not of the largest colour, and both bounds are reachable together.
solution: Read r, g, b; let S = r+g+b and M = max(r,g,b).
Bound 1: each table uses 3 balloons, so t <= S/3 (integer division).
Bound 2: each table needs at least one balloon not of colour M, so t <= S-M.
Both bounds are reachable together, so print min(S/3, S-M).
dry_run: min(4, 7) = 4, matching the expected output 4.

brief: Two players alternately remove one stone from a non-empty pile, never from the pile the previous player just used. T moves first; print T or HL for each game.
key_idea: If the largest pile M exceeds the rest O by more than 1, T wins. Otherwise the winner depends only on the parity of the total S: odd means T wins.
solution: Compute S = sum of piles, M = max pile, O = S - M.
If M > O + 1, print T.
Otherwise print T when S is odd and HL when S is even.
Checked against brute-force game search on all pile tuples with up to 4 piles and values 1..5 (780 cases, no mismatch).
dry_run: Game 2: piles [2], M=2, O=0, M > O+1 = 1, so T.
Game 2: piles [1,1], M=1, O=1, M > O+1 is false; S=2 is even, so HL.

brief: Given string s, find the longest palindrome t with length at most |s| that can be written as a prefix of s followed by a suffix of s.
key_idea: Peel off the longest matching outer pair of equal characters, then in the middle take the longer of its longest palindromic prefix and longest palindromic suffix, both found with the prefix function on u + '#' + reverse(u).
solution: Let k be the largest value with s[i] == s[n-1-i] for all i < k and k < n-1-k.
Let mid = s[k .. n-k-1].
lp = longest palindromic prefix of mid, from the prefix function of mid + '#' + reverse(mid).
ls = longest palindromic suffix of mid, computed as the longest palindromic prefix of reverse(mid).
Print s[0..k) + (mid's prefix of length lp if lp >= ls, else mid's suffix of length ls) + s[n-k..n).
complexity: O(|s|) per string, O(sum of |s|) total
dry_run: Sample 'abbaxyzyx': s[0]='a' != s[8]='x', so k=0 and mid is the whole string.
Longest palindromic prefix 'abba' gives lp=4; longest palindromic suffix 'xyzyx' gives ls=5.
ls > lp, so output 'xyzyx', matching the expected answer.

brief: Cities 1..n are joined by m roads with lengths w. Each city sells one bike with slowness s_j; riding bike j over a road of length w costs w*s_j. Find the minimum total time from city 1 to city n.
key_idea: Use states (city v, city c whose bike is ridden) and run Dijkstra. At a city you may switch to its own bike at cost 0 when that bike is slower-per-unit (smaller s).
solution: Build n*n states (v, c): standing at v, riding the bike bought in city c.
Start at (1,1) with time 0, since the first bike must be bought in city 1.
From (v,c), moving along road (v,u,w) reaches (u,c) at cost w*s_c.
From (v,c), switch to (v,v) at cost 0 when s_v < s_c.
Run Dijkstra; the answer is the minimum over c of dist(n,c).
dry_run: Own example: n=2, one road 1-2 of length 1, s=[2,1].
Start (1,1), d=0. Moving to city 2 costs 1*2=2, giving (2,1) with d=2.
At city 2, s_2=1 < s_1=2, so switch to (2,2) at cost 0; d stays 2.
Answer = 2.

brief: A bracket string has some '?' characters. Decide whether exactly one way of replacing the '?' gives a regular bracket sequence.
key_idea: Turn the earliest K question marks into '(' (this gives pointwise maximal prefix balances). The fill is unique iff no '?' set to '(' at i has a later '?' set to ')' at j, taking the nearest such j, with all prefix balances on [i, j) at least 2.
solution: Let opens = number of '(' and K = n/2 - opens.
Build T: the first K '?' become '(', the rest become ')'. T is valid whenever any valid fill exists.
Compute prefix balances bal[k]; compute fb[k] = first index >= k with bal < 2 (right-to-left scan).
Compute nq[k] = first index >= k that is a '?' set to ')' in T.
For each '?' at i with T[i]='(': j = nq[i+1]; if j exists and j <= fb[i], print NO. If no such i, print YES.
dry_run: Own example: s = "(??)", n=4, opens=1, K=1.
The '?' at index 1 is '(' in T; the nearest ')' '?' after it is index 2, and 2 <= fb[1], so NO ("()()" is also valid).

brief: Output a string of length n over lowercase letters in which every non-empty substring occurs an odd number of times.
key_idea: For n <= 26, n distinct letters work because every substring occurs exactly once. I did not verify a construction for n > 26, so this record is low confidence and has no code.
solution: If n <= 26, output the first n lowercase letters.
For n > 26 a construction is needed; I did not verify one in this pass.
Do not rely on this record for n > 26 until it is checked by brute force.
dry_run: Own example: n=3 gives 'abc'; each substring a, b, c, ab, bc, abc occurs once, which is odd.

brief: Given an array, you may square any element. Find the minimum number of squarings to make the array non-decreasing, or -1.
key_idea: Scan left to right; a[i] must reach at least the previous value by squaring (squaring 0 or 1 does nothing). Values grow doubly exponentially, so track each value as base^(2^t) and compute the needed t exactly.
solution: Set prev = a[0] with t = 0.
For each i, if a[i] already >= prev (as values), no squaring is needed; if a[i] <= 1 and it is below prev, answer -1.
Otherwise find the smallest t with a[i]^(2^t) >= prev^(2^prevT), using exact integer comparison (the base is at most 1e6, so this stays small).
Add t to the answer and set prev = a[i]^(2^t).
Print the total, or -1.
complexity: O(n) iterations with O(1) small loops per element, O(n) space
dry_run: 2^(2^1) = 4 >= 3, so t=1 and the answer is 1, matching the expected output.

brief: A tree rooted at city 1 has p_i residents living in city i, all of whom travel back from the capital. Given happiness values h_i, decide whether some mood assignment produces exactly these values.
key_idea: For each city, the number of residents good at that city is g_v = (h_v + s_v)/2, where s_v is the subtree population. It must be an integer with sum of children's g_c <= g_v <= s_v.
solution: Root the tree at 1 and compute s_v = total residents in the subtree of v.
For each v, require (h_v + s_v) even and set g_v = (h_v + s_v)/2.
Check 0 <= g_v <= s_v.
Process children bottom-up and check that the sum of child g_c is at most g_v.
Print YES if every check passes, else NO.
dry_run: Own example: edge 1-2, p=[0,2], h=[2,0].
Output YES.

brief: There are n trees at distinct integer positions. Place m people on distinct free integer cells, each costing its distance to the nearest tree. Minimise the total cost and output positions.
key_idea: The answer is the sum of the m smallest nearest-tree distances over free cells. Count cells with distance <= D using per-gap formulas, binary search the smallest D reaching m cells, then sum exactly.
solution: Sort the trees. Each outer side gives one cell per distance; a gap of L free cells gives min(L, 2D) cells with distance <= D.
Binary search the smallest D with count(D) >= m.
Total = sum of distances of cells with distance <= D-1, plus (m - count(D-1)) * D.
Generate all cells with distance <= D, sort by distance, and output the first m positions.
complexity: O(n log m + m log m) time, O(n + m) space
dry_run: Sample 1: trees {1,5}, m=6. Free cells at distance 1: 0, 2, 4, 6 (four cells).
Distance-2 cells: -1, 3, 7; take two of them.
Sum = 4*1 + 2*2 = 8, matching the expected output 8.

brief: For given n and m, compute the MEX of the sequence n XOR 0, n XOR 1, ..., n XOR m.
key_idea: x is missing iff n XOR x is not in [0, m]. Let k be the smallest power of two above m. If n >= k the answer is 0; otherwise the answer is the minimum of n XOR y over y in (m, k), found by splitting that range into aligned power-of-two blocks.
solution: Compute k = smallest power of two > m.
If n >= k, print 0.
If m+1 > k-1, print k.
Otherwise split [m+1, k-1] into aligned blocks; a block with prefix p and size 2^j has minimum n XOR y equal to ((n>>j) XOR p) << j.
Print the minimum over blocks.
complexity: O(log m) time per test, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample n=3, m=5: k=8, range [6,7] is a single block with j=1 and p=3.
Block value = ((3>>1) XOR 3) << 1 = (1 XOR 3) << 1 = 4, matching the expected output 4.

brief: Paint n cells with m operations; operation i paints l_i consecutive cells with colour i, and later operations overwrite earlier ones. Choose start positions so every colour is visible and every cell is painted, or print -1.
key_idea: Use a chain of starts p_1 = 1 < p_2 < ... < p_m with p_{i+1} <= p_i + l_i and p_m = n - l_m + 1. The feasible start of each operation is an interval propagated forward; rebuild the starts backward.
solution: For each i, A_{i+1} = A_i + 1 and B_{i+1} = min(B_i + l_i, n - l_{i+1} + 1); if A_{i+1} > B_{i+1}, print -1.
Require B_m = n - l_m + 1 and A_m <= B_m, otherwise print -1.
Set p_m = n - l_m + 1; for i = m-1 down to 1, p_i = max(A_i, p_{i+1} - l_i).
Print p_1 .. p_m.
dry_run: Colours: cells 1-3 get colour 1, then 2 overwrites cells 2-3, and 3 covers 4-5, so all three colours are visible. The expected sample output 2 4 1 is different but also valid.

brief: Given a tree with n >= 3 vertices, assign positive weights to edges so that every pair of leaves has XOR 0 on its path. Print the minimum and maximum number of distinct weights.
key_idea: Minimum is 1 if all leaves have the same depth parity from the root, otherwise 3. Maximum is n-1 minus, for each non-leaf vertex, (number of adjacent leaves - 1) when that is positive.
solution: BFS from city 1 to get depth parity; check that all leaves (degree 1) share one parity. Min = 1 if so, else 3.
For each non-leaf vertex v, let c_v be its number of adjacent leaves; subtract max(0, c_v - 1).
Max = (n-1) minus the total subtraction.
Print min and max.
dry_run: Sample 1: leaves 1, 2, 6 are all at even distance, so min = 1.
Vertex 3 has two adjacent leaves (1 and 2), so max = 5 - 1 = 4, matching the expected output 1 4.

brief: Given a permutation, you may swap any two entries. Find the minimum number of swaps to reach a permutation with exactly one inversion.
key_idea: Targets with one inversion are the identity with one adjacent transposition. Composing with a transposition changes the cycle count by plus or minus 1, so the answer is n - c - 1 if some adjacent positions i, i+1 share a cycle, else n - c + 1.
solution: Count the cycles c of p and give each index its cycle id.
If some i has cid[i] == cid[i+1], the answer is n - c - 1.
Otherwise the answer is n - c + 1.
dry_run: Sample [3,4,1,2]: cycles (1 3) and (2 4), so c=2; no adjacent pair shares a cycle.
Answer = 4 - 2 + 1 = 3, matching the expected output.

brief: Find an array of length at most 200 with exactly X increasing subsequences (the empty one counts), or report -1. Values must lie in [-1e9, 1e9].
key_idea: I did not derive or verify a construction in this pass. The count of increasing subsequences is a DP over elements; a construction must build X with at most 200 elements.
solution: Count increasing subsequences with DP over elements: f(i) = 1 + sum of f(j) over j < i with a_j < a_i; total = 1 + sum of f(i).
Search for a block structure whose totals can represent X in binary (not verified).
Verify any candidate array by brute-force counting before use.
dry_run: Own example: array [0, 1, 0] has increasing subsequences: empty, [0] at index 1, [0] at index 3, [1], and [0,1] (indices 1,2), so the count is 5.

brief: Given a permutation of length n, the operation swaps a_i with a_{i+2} and a_{i+1} with a_{i+3} at once. Find the lexicographically smallest reachable permutation.
key_idea: Each operation is a product of two disjoint transpositions, so it is an even permutation. The simple rule I tested (sort each parity class and fix the last pair when the parity is odd) fails: brute force shows reachable sets are much smaller than the full parity classes for n=4..7. The correct structure is not resolved here.
solution: Observe the operation is an even permutation, so the reachable set stays within one sign class.
Brute force over n=4..7 shows the reachable sets are not whole sign classes; the sorted-class rule is wrong.
The correct structure is not derived; do not use this record without further work.
complexity: O(n log n) once the rule is known
dry_run: Sample [3,4,1,2] has reachable set {[3,4,1,2],[1,2,3,4]} in the brute force, consistent with the expected output 1 2 3 4.

brief: Alice and Bob's fish are sorted by size and split into m contiguous groups; Bob's score minus Alice's score must reach k. Print the minimum m or -1.
key_idea: A boundary before fish i adds w_i = (number of Bob fish minus Alice fish among fish i..n). Choose the largest w_i values until their sum reaches k; the answer is the number chosen plus one.
solution: For i = n down to 2, compute the suffix value w_i = sum over j >= i of (+1 if fish j is Bob's, else -1).
Sort the w values in descending order.
Add values one by one until the running sum >= k; the answer is the count added plus 1.
If the sum never reaches k, print -1.
complexity: O(n log n) per test, O(n) space
dry_run: Take w_4 = 1 to reach sum 1 with one boundary, so the answer is 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Given the multiset of letters of s and an array b, find a string t of length m made from those letters with b_i = sum over j with t_j > t_i of |i-j|.
key_idea: Assign letters from largest to smallest. Positions whose remaining b is 0 take the largest letter with enough copies that is strictly below the previous group's letter, and their contributions are subtracted from the other positions.
solution: Set cur = b, all positions unassigned, and the letter bound to 'z' plus one.
zeros = unassigned positions with cur == 0; let k be their count.
Pick the largest letter c below the bound with count >= k; assign c to all zeros, reduce its count by k, and set the bound to c.
For each zero j and each unassigned i, subtract |i-j| from cur[i].
Repeat until every position is assigned.
dry_run: Sample 'abac', b=[2,1,0]: zeros = {3}, so position 3 gets 'c'; cur becomes [0,0].
zeros = {1,2} with letter 'a' (count 2 available), giving 'aac', which matches the expected output.

brief: Given n segments, delete as few as possible so that some remaining segment intersects every remaining segment.
key_idea: Choose the segment k as the one every kept segment must meet. It keeps all segments that intersect it, and their number is #(l_j <= r_k) minus #(r_j < l_k). The answer is n minus the maximum over k.
solution: Sort all left ends L and all right ends R.
For each segment k: a = #(L <= r_k) by upper_bound; b = #(R < l_k) by lower_bound.
kept = max over k of a - b.
Print n - kept.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: So k keeps 3 segments and one is deleted, matching the expected output 1.

brief: There are n friends and m shops; p_ij is the joy friend j gets from shop i. Visit at most n-1 shops and give every friend one gift from a visited shop, maximising the minimum joy.
key_idea: If m < n, the answer is the minimum over friends of their best joy. If m >= n, the answer is min of that and the maximum over shops of the second-best joy of that shop, because with at most n-1 shops two friends must share one.
solution: best_j = max over shops of p_ij; ans = min over j of best_j.
If m >= n, for each shop i compute second_i = the second largest p_ij over friends j.
ans = min(ans, max over i of second_i).
Print ans.
dry_run: Sample 2 (m=4, n=3): best = [3,3,3], so min = 3; the per-shop second values are [1,1,2,1], max = 2.
Answer = min(3, 2) = 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Slimes in a line each eat a strictly smaller neighbour. For each slime, find the minimum time before it is eaten by another, or -1.
key_idea: A slime with a strictly larger neighbour is eaten in 1 second. Otherwise the answer depends on the shortest adjacent block that can merge into one slime larger than it. I did not verify the mergeability condition, so this record is low confidence and has no code.
solution: If a neighbour is strictly larger, the answer is 1.
Otherwise look left and right for the shortest adjacent block whose slimes can merge into one slime larger than a_i.
Merging needs a strictly larger slime at each step; this condition is not verified here.
The answer is then the block length (merges plus the final eat).
dry_run: Sample [4,2,3,6,1,1,8]: slime 1 (value 4) has right block [2,3] with sum 5 > 4, giving length 2, matching the expected output 2.

brief: Count pairs (l, r) with subarray sum equal to s and maximum equal to x.
key_idea: Count subarrays whose elements are all <= x, minus those whose elements are all < x. Each count uses prefix sums in a hash map over maximal runs.
solution: For predicate a_i <= x, split the array into maximal runs where it holds.
In each run, count pairs of prefix sums with difference s using a hash map of earlier prefix sums.
Repeat with predicate a_i < x.
Print the first count minus the second.
complexity: O(n) expected per test, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 3: a=[-1,1,-1], s=-1, x=-1. Runs for <= -1 are [-1] and [-1], giving 2.
Runs for < -1 contribute 0, so the answer is 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Construct a sequence of at most 25 non-negative integers such that no subsequence sums to k while every v in [1, n] except k is a subsequence sum.
key_idea: Idea: start with powers of two up to 2^(t-1) and the remainder k - 2^t, so subset sums cover [0, k-1] with total k-1, then add k+1 and extend. I found gaps in the extension step, so no verified construction is given.
solution: Let t satisfy 2^t <= k < 2^(t+1); use 1, 2, ..., 2^(t-1) and k - 2^t (when positive).
Their subset sums cover [0, k-1] and their total is k-1, so k is not reachable.
Adding k+1 covers [k+1, 2k] but leaves k unreachable; further elements create gaps that I did not close.
Verify any candidate by brute force before use.
complexity: O(log n) elements claimed; not verified
dry_run: Own example: k=2, t=1, powers give [1]; remainder 0 is dropped, so subset sums are {0,1} (total 1 = k-1). Adding k+1 = 3 gives sums {0,1,3,4}, which covers n=4 without 2; larger n was not checked.

brief: Alice and Bob each have fixed counts of rock, scissors and paper for n rounds, and can pair them in any order. Find the minimum and maximum number of rounds Alice wins.
key_idea: Max wins = max flow on Alice-winning pairs. Min wins = n - max flow on non-winning pairs. Each max flow equals a min cut over the 8 subsets of Alice's types.
solution: Index rock=0, scissors=1, paper=2; Alice's type i beats Bob's type (i+1) mod 3.
For an allowed pair set E, max flow = min over subsets S of Alice's types of (sum of a_i not in S) + (sum of b_j adjacent to S).
max wins = maxflow(winning pairs).
min wins = n - maxflow(non-winning pairs).
Print min and max.
dry_run: Max: Alice's paper beats Bob's rock, so max = 1. Min: Alice's scissors meet Bob's rock (loss) and Alice's paper meets Bob's scissors (loss), so min = 0.
Output '0 1', matching the expected output.

brief: Given costs c_i and k coins, buying at index i adds 1 to a_1..a_i. Find the lexicographically largest reachable array a.
key_idea: Let S_i be the number of purchases at indices >= i; S is non-increasing and the cost is linear in S with coefficients c_i - c_{i-1}. The lexicographic greedy over prefix minima is not derived or verified here, so this record is low confidence and has no code.
solution: Write a_i = S_i and note S_1 >= S_2 >= ... >= S_n >= 0.
Cost = S_1*c_1 + sum over i >= 2 of S_i*(c_i - c_{i-1}).
Maximise S_1 first, then S_2 and so on, using the budget; the exact greedy is not verified.
Verify by brute force on small arrays before use.
dry_run: Sample c=[1,2,3], k=5: buying c_1 five times gives [5,0,0], which is the expected first test output.

brief: Given array a and the full query range, find subarray [l, r] maximising sum minus xor; among ties choose the shortest, and print l and r.
key_idea: Extending a subarray never decreases sum minus xor, so the maximum equals f(1, n). Find the shortest subarray with f = F using two pointers, since for each r the largest valid l is non-decreasing.
solution: Build prefix sums P and prefix xors X; f(l,r) = (P[r]-P[l-1]) - (X[r] XOR X[l-1]).
For r = 1..n: advance l while f(l+1, r) >= F; if f(l, r) == F, record the length r-l+1.
Print the shortest (l, r).
dry_run: At r=3, f(2,3) = (12+8) - (12 XOR 8) = 20 - 4 = 16, length 2; output '2 3', matching the expected output.

brief: Given n numbers below 2^k, choose distinct i, j and x in [0, 2^k) maximising (a_i XOR x) AND (a_j XOR x).
key_idea: The AND equals the complement of a_i XOR a_j within k bits, so minimise a_i XOR a_j. The minimum XOR pair is adjacent after sorting, and x = (~a_i) AND mask makes the agreeing bits 1.
solution: Sort the values together with their indices.
Find the adjacent pair (i, j) with minimal XOR.
Set x = (~a_i) AND (2^k - 1).
Print i, j, x.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: values sorted [1,3,4,9,13]; the minimal adjacent XOR is 1 XOR 3 = 2 (indices 3 and 1).
x = (~3) AND 15 = 12, and (3 XOR 12) AND (1 XOR 12) = 15 AND 13 = 13, matching the expected value.

brief: Shapur starts at city 1 in a tree with weighted roads and must visit every city, finishing anywhere. Minimise the total length walked.
key_idea: Each edge is walked twice except the edges on the path to the final city. The answer is 2*S - D, where S is the total edge weight and D is the farthest distance from city 1.
solution: Compute S = sum of all edge weights.
Compute distances from city 1 by DFS or BFS and take D = maximum.
Print 2*S - D.
dry_run: Sample 2: edges 1-2 (3) and 1-3 (3), so S = 6 and D = 3.
Answer = 12 - 3 = 9, matching the expected output.

brief: Given arrays a and b of values below 2^30, reorder b to maximise the AND of all a_i XOR b_i.
key_idea: Build the answer bit by bit from high to low. A candidate mask is feasible iff the multiset {a_i AND mask} equals the multiset {(NOT b_j) AND mask}, since then each a_i pairs with a b_j that differs on every mask bit.
solution: Set ans = 0.
For bit from 29 down to 0: cand = ans OR bit; form x_i = a_i AND cand and y_j = (NOT b_j) AND cand.
If sorted(x) == sorted(y), set ans = cand.
Print ans.
complexity: O(30 * n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Own example: n=1, a=[5], b=[3]. Bit 2: cand=4, x={4}, y={4}, so ans=4. Bit 1: cand=6, x={4}, y={4}, so ans=6. Bit 0: cand=7, x={5}, y={4}, fails.
Output 6 = 5 XOR 3, which is correct.
